passages.original: postea Gai Caesaris et deinde Augusti cognomen assumpsit, alterum testamento maioris auunculi, alterum Munati Planci sententia, cum quibusdam censentibus Romulum appellari oportere quasi et ipsum conditorem urbis, praeualuisset, ut Augustus potius uocaretur, non tantum nouo sed etiam ampliore cognomine, quod loca quoque religiosa et in quibus augurato quid consecratur augusta dicantur, ab auctu uel ab auium gestu gustuue, sicut etiam Ennius docet scribens:
passages.english: Afterwards he took the surname of Gaius Caesar and then that of Augustus, the one under the will of his great-uncle, the other on the motion of Munatius Plancus. For when some were of the opinion that he ought to be called Romulus, as being himself also a founder of the city, [Plancus's view] prevailed that he should rather be called Augustus, a surname not only new but also more dignified, since places that are sacred, and those in which anything is consecrated after the taking of auguries, are also called *augusta* ("august"), from *auctus* ("increase") or from the movement or feeding of birds (*avium gestus gustusve*), as Ennius also teaches when he writes:
passages.notes: The sentence is somewhat loosely constructed: the subject of 'praevaluisset' (prevailed) is understood from 'Munati Planci sententia' (the motion of Plancus). The etymologies turn on Latin wordplay (augustus from auctus, or from avium gestus/gustus, linked to augury).
